# Introduction

Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) is used to test theories about constructs and how they relate to each other

- useful for theory testing and development
- model-building can be separated into 2 parts:
  1. measurement model - how observed measures relate to underlying constructs
  2. structural model - how the constructs relate to each other
- both parts can technically be estimated at the same time
  - authors argue the measurement model should be evaluated first
  - then the measurement and structural models can be evaluated together
- separating them helps researchers:
  - better assess construct validity
  - understand where poor model fit is coming from
  - avoid misleading interpretations
- measurement model helps assess:
  - convergent validity
  - discriminant validity
- structural model helps assess nomological validity once acceptable measurement has been established

# Background

## Exploratory Versus Confirmatory Analyses

Exploratory and confirmatory analysis are not completely separate and are better thought of as a progression

- exploratory factor analysis:
  - no required specification of the number of factors beforehand
- researchers can move toward confirmation by:
  - specifying the expected number of factors
  - testing how well the resulting model fits the data
- confirmatory factor analysis:
  - measurement model is specified beforehand
  - parameter values are still estimated from the data
- authors say "restricted analysis" may sometimes be a better description than purely confirmatory analysis
  - many parameters are restricted beforehand, usually to zero
- initial measurement models often do not fit well
  - researchers usually respecify and reestimate them using the same data
  - because of this, the process is rarely completely confirmatory
- strongest confirmation comes from cross-validating the final model using another sample

## Complementary Approaches for Theory Testing Versus Predictive Application

SEM methods can be chosen depending on whether the goal is theory testing or prediction

- Maximum Likelihood (ML) and Generalized Least Squares (GLS):
  - more useful for theory testing and development
  - based on the common factor model
  - separate random error and measure-specific variance from the latent construct
  - focus on explaining covariance between observed variables
  - provide:
    - efficient parameter estimates
    - overall model-fit testing
- one drawback:
  - factor scores are not defined exactly
  - not a major issue for theory testing
  - can reduce predictive accuracy

Partial Least Squares (PLS) is more useful for prediction and application

- treats all observed variance as useful variance
- focuses on maximizing explained variance
- produces exact component scores
  - useful for predicting individuals' standings
- limitations:
  - does not directly assess unidimensionality
  - does not provide an overall model-fit test
  - parameter estimates are less efficient than full-information methods
  - relationships among latent variables may be underestimated

Authors view ML/GLS and PLS as complementary

- ML or GLS - theory testing and development
- PLS - prediction and application
- rest of article focuses on ML/GLS for confirmatory theory testing

## Estimation Methods

Maximum Likelihood (ML) was the main estimation method used in SEM at the time

- under multivariate normality and large samples, ML estimates are:
  - unbiased
  - consistent
  - efficient
- allows researchers to test:
  - individual parameter significance
  - overall model fit using chi-square

Problem with ML:

- parameter estimates can still be fairly robust when normality is moderately violated
- standard errors and chi-square fit tests can become inaccurate
  - peaked distributions can cause models to be rejected too often
  - flatter distributions can create the opposite problem

Newer estimation methods were developed to reduce reliance on multivariate normality

- Generalized Least Squares (GLS)
- Asymptotically Distribution-Free (ADF) methods
- Weighted Least Squares (WLS)
- Diagonally Weighted Least Squares (DWLS)
- elliptical estimation

These more flexible methods also have drawbacks

- can require much larger sample sizes
- may require more computation
- ADF methods especially can become difficult with many observed variables

Authors say researchers should choose estimation methods based on:

- how reasonable the normality assumption is
- sample size
- model size
- limitations of the alternative estimation methods

# Confirmatory Measurement Model

Confirmatory measurement model shows how observed variables relate to underlying constructs

- used to determine whether the constructs are being measured properly
- constructs are allowed to correlate with each other
- this is evaluated before testing the structural relationships

## Need for Unidimensional Measurement

Unidimensionality means that a set of indicators should measure one underlying construct

- necessary before assigning a clear meaning to a latent construct
- assessed using:
  - internal consistency
  - external consistency
- multiple indicators are preferred because they help define constructs more clearly
- indicators that load on multiple constructs can make interpretation difficult

## Specification

Specification is the process of deciding how indicators and constructs are represented in the measurement model

- multiple indicators per construct are preferred
- researchers also need to consider:
  - how the factor scale is set
  - whether any constructs only have one indicator
  - whether the sample size is large enough
- around 150 observations is often enough for models with 3+ indicators per factor

## Assessment of Fit

After estimating the measurement model, researchers evaluate how well it fits the data

- overall fit can be assessed with statistics such as:
  - chi-square
  - goodness-of-fit index
  - root-mean-square residual
- convergent validity - indicators should significantly relate to the construct they are supposed to measure
- discriminant validity - different constructs should be meaningfully distinct from each other

## Respecification

Respecification means modifying the model when the original measurement model does not fit well

- changes should be based on theory and content, not statistics alone
- possible changes:
  - move an indicator to another factor
  - remove an indicator
  - allow an indicator to load on multiple factors
  - correlate measurement errors
- moving or removing indicators is preferred because it better preserves unidimensionality
- adding cross-loadings or correlated errors can improve fit but may make constructs harder to interpret

# One-Step Versus Two-Step Modeling Approaches

## The Confirmatory Structural Model

Confirmatory structural model tests the hypothesized relationships among latent constructs

- focuses on how the constructs affect or relate to each other
- differs from the measurement model:
  - measurement model - how observed indicators relate to constructs
  - structural model - how the constructs relate to each other
- 2 types of constructs:
  - endogenous - the causes are included within the model
  - exogenous - the causes are outside the model and are not explained

One-step approach estimates the measurement and structural models at the same time

- can create interpretational confounding when the model is misspecified
- interpretational confounding - the empirical meaning of a latent construct changes depending on how the structural model is specified
  - factor loadings may change when different structural models are tested
  - could improve overall fit while making the constructs harder to interpret
- this can make it unclear whether poor fit comes from:
  - bad measurement
  - incorrect structural relationships

Estimating the measurement model first helps reduce interpretational confounding

- no structural restrictions are imposed while the constructs are first being evaluated
- once acceptable unidimensional measurement is established, factor loadings should not change much when different structural models are tested
- helps preserve the intended meaning of the constructs

## Recommended Two-Step Modeling Approach

Two-step approach evaluates measurement before testing the structural relationships

1. evaluate the measurement model
   - determine whether observed indicators properly measure their constructs
   - establish acceptable:
     - unidimensionality
     - convergent validity
     - discriminant validity
     - overall model fit
   - respecify measurement problems before moving forward

2. evaluate the structural model
   - test the theoretical relationships among the constructs
   - assess whether the proposed structural model fits
   - contributes to assessment of nomological validity

Authors recommend comparing a series of nested structural models

- nested model - a more restricted version of another model
  - one or more freely estimated parameters are constrained
  - usually fixed at zero

5 models are used:

- Mn = null structural model
  - all relationships among constructs are fixed at zero
  - most restricted model
- Mc = constrained alternative model
  - one or more paths estimated in the theoretical model are constrained
  - represents a simpler theoretical alternative
- Mt = theoretical model
  - the researcher's main proposed model
- Mu = unconstrained alternative model
  - one or more paths restricted in Mt are freely estimated
  - represents a more complex theoretical alternative
- Ms = saturated model
  - all possible relationships among constructs are estimated
  - least restricted model
  - equivalent to the final measurement model

models are ordered:

Mn < Mc < Mt < Mu < Ms

Pseudo chi-square test is used first to determine whether any structural model could provide acceptable fit

- uses information from the saturated measurement model and null structural model
- if the test indicates no structural model could fit adequately:
  - suggests there may still be a fundamental problem with the measurement model
  - measurement model should be reconsidered before continuing
- a one-step approach would make this problem harder to identify

Sequential Chi-Square Difference Tests (SCDTs) compare nested structural models

- determine whether one model explains the construct relationships significantly better than another
- compare more constrained and less constrained models
- if the added paths do not significantly improve the model:
  - prefer the more constrained / simpler model
- if the added paths significantly improve explanation:
  - the more complex model may be necessary
- allows the theoretical model to be compared against realistic alternative explanations

Comparing Mt with Ms helps assess nomological validity

- asks whether the proposed theoretical relationships adequately explain the relationships among the constructs
- measurement model acts as the baseline for comparison

Two-step approach also emphasizes degrees of freedom and strength of theoretical explanation

- a model with every possible path estimated may fit well
  - but provides very little ability to make meaningful theoretical or causal claims
- theory becomes more informative when it successfully predicts that some paths should not exist

## Advantages of the Two-Step Approach

Two-step approach makes it easier to determine where poor model fit is coming from

- measurement model is evaluated first
- structural model is evaluated only after acceptable measurement is established
- helps separate:
  - measurement problems
  - theoretical / structural problems

Reduces interpretational confounding

- constructs are defined before structural relationships are imposed
- reduces the chance that changing structural paths changes the meaning of the constructs

Prevents good fit in one part of the model from hiding poor fit in another

- one-step approach evaluates measurement and structural components together
- strong fit in one part can potentially compensate for weak fit in the other
- separate evaluation makes problems easier to detect

Allows formal comparisons between competing theoretical models

- researcher does not only ask whether Mt fits
- compares Mt with:
  - a more constrained alternative
  - a less constrained alternative
  - the saturated measurement model
- helps test rival explanations rather than assuming the original theory is correct

Encourages parsimony

- more complex models usually fit better because more paths are estimated
- extra paths should only be included if they meaningfully improve explanation
- if 2 models explain the data similarly:
  - prefer the simpler model

Absent paths can also provide theoretical information

- support for a path being fixed at zero can support the theory
- theory includes both:
  - relationships that should exist
  - relationships that should not exist

Highlights the tradeoff between model fit and strength of causal inference

- adding more paths can improve fit
- adding too many paths weakens the ability to make meaningful causal or theoretical claims
- a highly flexible model may fit well but provide little theoretical explanation

Other advantages summarized by the authors:

- allows significance testing of all factor loadings
- can determine whether any structural model would provide acceptable fit
- allows an independent test of the proposed theoretical model
- provides a framework for comparing the theoretical model with likely alternatives

## Additional Considerations in Structural Model Interpretation

### Practical vs Statistical Significance

Statistical significance does not always mean a difference is practically important

- chi-square statistics are affected by sample size
- with large samples:
  - very small differences can become statistically significant
  - two models may be statistically different even if the practical difference is minor

Normed Fit Index (NFI) can be used with statistical tests

- ranges from 0 to 1
- represents how much observed covariance is explained compared with a null model
- helps determine whether differences between models are practically meaningful

Researchers may sometimes prefer a simpler model even if a more complex model is statistically better

- if the improvement in fit is very small
- simpler model may still provide an adequate explanation
- again emphasizes parsimony

### Considerations in Drawing Causal Inferences

Good model fit does not prove that a theory is true

- models are not confirmed by data
- they gain support when the data fails to disconfirm them
- other models may fit equally well

Temporal order does not automatically prove causation

- one variable occurring before another does not mean it caused it
- correlation and timing alone are not enough

Naming a latent construct does not mean it is perfectly understood

- observed indicators may not perfectly represent the construct because of:
  - invalidity - indicator measures something other than what was intended
  - unreliability - part of the observed value comes from random measurement error

Respecification reduces the strength of causal conclusions

- modifying a model based on the same data makes the process increasingly exploratory
- strong confirmatory claims become harder to justify

Cross-validation would ideally be used

- develop the model using one sample
- validate it using a separate sample
- often difficult because SEM already requires fairly large samples

Most causal interpretations from SEM should therefore be qualified

- acceptable fit provides support for a proposed explanation
- it does not prove causality

# Conclusion

Anderson and Gerbing argue that SEM should generally use a two-step approach instead of estimating the measurement and structural models at the same time

1. evaluate the measurement model
  - make sure indicators adequately measure their intended constructs
  - establish unidimensionality, convergent validity, and discriminant validity
2. evaluate the structural model
  - test the hypothesized relationships among the constructs
  - assess nomological validity

The main advantage of the two-step approach is that it separates measurement problems from structural problems

- reduces interpretational confounding
- prevents good fit in one part of the model from hiding poor fit in another
- allows researchers to compare the proposed theory with plausible alternative models
- supports more meaningful interpretation of constructs and relationships

SEM can be very useful for theory testing and construct validation when used carefully

- researchers should not rely only on statistical fit
- model respecification should be supported by theory
- good model fit does not prove causality
- causal conclusions should usually remain qualified

# References

Anderson, James C., and David W. Gerbing. 1988. “Structural Equation Modeling in Practice: A Review and Recommended Two-Step Approach.” *Psychological Bulletin* 103 (3): 411–423. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.103.3.411.
